title: Revelations Research Ltd. (1991 TCC) Tax Court Case
subject: TCC appeal on whether a 'Synthetic Intelligence' neural-network project qualified as SR&ED for a Part VIII refund.
outcome: Appeal dismissed; the court preferred the Crown's expert and found no cogent evidence of systematic investigation.
summary: Revelations Research Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue, a 1991 Tax Court of Canada decision, rejected a Canadian corporation's claim that its "Synthetic Intelligence" neural-network project was SR&ED qualifying for a Part VIII refund for its 1986 taxation year. Key takeaway: ambitious AI work does not qualify without cogent evidence of a systematic investigation by means of experiment or analysis.

body.text: Section 1: Executive Summary and Case Background
Procedural Posture and the Taxpayer's Claim

The decision of the Tax Court of Canada in Revelations Research Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue stands as an early and enduring cornerstone of Canadian jurisprudence governing Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentives. Heard before the Tax Court of Canada by Associate Chief Judge Christie under Court No. 89-1001, with judgment delivered on December 6, 1991, and subsequently reported at [1992] 1 C.T.C. 2136 and 92 D.T.C. 1036, the appeal concerned an assessment of tax under Part VIII of the Income Tax Act for the appellant's 1986 taxation year, which ran from May 22, 1985 to May 21, 1986. The appellant, Revelations Research Ltd., was a Canadian corporation that had been assessed Part VIII tax of $15,750,000 (50 per cent of a $31,500,000 amount designated under subsection 194(1) of the Act, in a transaction of the kind commonly referred to as a "quick flip"), plus interest, and that claimed entitlement to a Part VIII refund under subsection 194(2) in respect of activities it characterized as scientific research and experimental development in the field of artificial intelligence (AI), namely a neural-network project labelled "Synthetic Intelligence".

During the 1986 taxation year, the corporate appellant asserted that it was engaged in a "Synthetic Intelligence" project whose ultimate objective was to develop a hardware system constructed of elements similar to biological neurons, capable of performing non-numerical functions such as pattern recognition and rule interpretation. At the hearing before the Tax Court of Canada, the evidentiary foundation for the appellant's claim rested heavily upon the oral testimony of the company's president, W.E. Madryga, and on three volumes of documents he assembled for the appeal (dated September 20, 1991), supplemented by the opinion evidence of two expert witnesses called by the appellant, Professor Martin Snelgrove and Dr. Donald F. Rennick. The taxpayer relied exclusively on its project falling within paragraph 2900(1)(c) of the Income Tax Regulations (development, namely the use of the results of basic or applied research for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes), contending that its work therefore qualified as scientific research and experimental development giving rise to a Part VIII refund under the Income Tax Act (Canada).
The Minister's Challenge and the Battle of Technical Experts

The Respondent, the Minister of National Revenue, assessed the appellant for Part VIII tax for the 1986 taxation year and took the position that the appellant was not entitled to a Part VIII refund, which depends on expenditures on scientific research and experimental development described in subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i) and 37(1)(b)(i). The Minister's assessment was predicated on the determination that Revelations Research Ltd. had failed to demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that it had actually carried out a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis during the taxation year in issue. Rather than accepting the appellant's self-characterization of its activities as artificial intelligence research, the Crown challenged both the scientific methodology employed by the taxpayer and the evidentiary sufficiency of its technical records.

A defining feature of the trial before the Tax Court of Canada was the prominent role played by expert witnesses. In addition to hearing testimony from the president of Revelations Research Ltd., the presiding judge heard and evaluated evidence from three witnesses whom the Court found qualified to give expert opinion evidence, all of them learned in the field of computer science: two called by the appellant (Dr. Rennick, who knew Mr. Madryga from the University of Toronto but stated that he had no business relationship with him and received no fee for his opinion, and Professor Snelgrove, who had previously worked with Mr. Madryga at the Computer Research Facility) and one called by the respondent. The expert witnesses were Professor Martin Snelgrove, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering at the University of Toronto (Ph.D. in electrical engineering, 1982) whose special pursuit is signal processing; Dr. Donald F. Rennick, a principal with Cantech International, a division of Naress Associates Ltd., formerly with Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd., holding a doctorate in mechanical engineering from the University of Toronto (1974), who was found qualified as an expert regarding data acquisition and real-time systems but not in respect of neural networks; and Dr. Peter C. Davies of Expert Solutions of Toronto, who held a doctorate in mathematics from the University of Toronto (1979) and specializes in artificial intelligence, neural networks and expert systems.

The expert testimony presented the Court with a sharp divergence in analytical methodology. Professor Snelgrove submitted a short report dated October 21, 1991, applying the criteria of Revenue Canada Information Circular 86-4R2, in which he stated that, because his own area was signal processing, he could not comment in detail on the overall project; he concluded that the part of the activity he could clearly judge, the data acquisition, was clearly qualified, while the overall project was harder for him to judge, although he saw no "Negative Indicators". Dr. Rennick, also called by the appellant, filed a report dated October 21, 1991, which took the information presented to him by Mr. Madryga at face value and concluded that the project appeared to meet all three criteria, while acknowledging that the ten-year plan was a series of milestones rather than a written series of items to try and that Mr. Madryga had shredded all working papers for reasons of commercial security; conversely, Dr. Davies, retained by Revenue Canada, met with Mr. Madryga and examined documentation originating with the appellant and material supplied by Revenue Canada. Most decisively, Dr. Davies' report dated July 14, 1988, concluded that he found no part of the appellant's project to be eligible as scientific research or experimental development, and at trial he reaffirmed that evaluation, testifying that the only plan he found (the ten-year plan overview) was a list of goals rather than a research plan, that he received no information setting out initial hypotheses or any means of testing them, that detailed notes of research work were not produced, that the work was not carried out in any systematic, scientific manner, that the research team was inadequate in size and credentials, and that nothing significant had been accomplished.
Governing Canadian Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The legal dispute in Revelations Research Ltd. was adjudicated under the interlocking provisions of the Income Tax Act (Canada) and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations as applicable to the 1986 taxation year. Under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, taxpayers were permitted to deduct expenditures of a current nature (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i)) and of a capital nature (subparagraph 37(1)(b)(i)) made in Canada, directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer and related to its business, on "scientific research and experimental development" carried on in Canada. Concurrently, subsections 127(5) and 127(9), alongside section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, related to the Investment Tax Credit regime for qualified SR&ED expenditures (including the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9)); however, the provision actually in issue in Revelations Research was the Part VIII refund defined in subsection 194(2), which is calculated by reference to the corporation's scientific research and experimental development tax credit and to expenditures claimed under paragraph 37(1)(a) or (b), and which cross-references subsections 127(5) and 127(9).

At the time of the 1986 taxation year, the substantive legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" was codified in subsection 2900(1) of the Income Tax Regulations (subsequently migrated into subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act in later legislative consolidations). Regulation 2900(1) defined SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis," categorized into three eligible branches: basic research undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view under paragraph 2900(1)(a); applied research undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view under paragraph 2900(1)(b); and development, namely the use of the results of basic or applied research for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, under paragraph 2900(1)(c), which was the only branch on which the appellant relied.

Where a project satisfied the foundational test under paragraphs 2900(1)(a), (b), or (c), the closing words of subsection 2900(1) included activities with respect to engineering or design, operations research, mathematical analysis or computer programming and psychological research, where such activities were undertaken directly in support of the activities described in paragraph (a), (b) or (c) (the "commensurate with the needs" qualifier and a separate paragraph (d) for supporting work appear only in the later version of the definition). Conversely, paragraphs 2900(1)(d) to (j) excluded activities with respect to market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices or products; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring or drilling for or producing minerals, petroleum or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection. During this era, administrative interpretation by the Department of National Revenue (now the Canada Revenue Agency) was guided by Information Circular IC 86-4 (in particular IC 86-4R2 dated August 29, 1988, which post-dated the year under review but dealt with subsection 2900(1) and was relied upon by the appellant's experts), Scientific Research and Experimental Development (later revised as IC 86-4R3 in 1994, and since replaced by the CRA's Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy, first published in 2012, and the current Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives dated August 13, 2021), which articulated the three core criteria of scientific or technological advancement, scientific or technological uncertainty, and scientific and technical content.
The Tax Court's Final Holding and Jurisprudential Legacy

Upon weighing the oral testimony of the corporate president alongside the competing reports and testimony of the three expert witnesses, the Tax Court of Canada dismissed the appeal, holding that it fell to be decided by the weight or credibility of the evidence and accepting Dr. Davies' evaluation over that of the appellant's witnesses. The Court held that Revelations Research Ltd.'s artificial intelligence projects did not qualify as scientific research or experimental development within the meaning of the Income Tax Act and section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations, having found that it had not been established that there was any systematic investigation or research of the nature described in Sass Manufacturing Ltd., thereby upholding the Minister's Part VIII assessment and the denial of a Part VIII refund for the 1986 taxation year.

The significance of Revelations Research Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue extends far beyond its immediate disposition of the appellant's 1986 tax refund. In Canadian tax law, the decision applied the systematic-investigation standard articulated in Sass Manufacturing Ltd. to determine whether a "scientific experiment" has genuinely been conducted. Operating in tandem with the earlier Tax Court ruling in Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue (88 D.T.C. 1363), Revelations Research bridged the gap between traditional industrial manufacturing R&D and intangible computer science and artificial intelligence claims. The decision has been cited in subsequent Tax Court of Canada SR&ED rulings, including the following four (in Data Kinetics, for example, it was cited, alongside Sass and Canalerta, as one of the decisions emphasizing the words "systematic investigation or search", in an appeal that was ultimately allowed): Canalerta Technologies Inc. v. Minister of National Revenue, [1992] T.C.J. No. 623, 93 D.T.C. 1651; Hadad v. Minister of National Revenue, [1994] T.C.J. No. 409; Promac Informatique Inc. v. R., [1997] 2 C.T.C. 2940; and Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 4 C.T.C. 2618, 98 D.T.C. 1877. Within this line of Canadian jurisprudence, Revelations Research stands for the strict legal proposition that conceptual ambition in an advanced technological domain cannot substitute for objective, empirical proof of systematic experimentation.

body.text: Section 2: Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures
Failure to Establish a Systematic Investigation by Means of Experiment or Analysis

The primary legal failure that doomed the appellant's claim in Revelations Research Ltd. was its inability to satisfy the threshold statutory requirement of a "systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" under subsection 2900(1) of the Income Tax Regulations. In Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence, the phrase "by means of experiment or analysis" is not merely descriptive; it establishes a mandatory methodological condition. Following the standard articulated by Judge Sarchuk in Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue (88 D.T.C. 1363), the Tax Court of Canada requires a taxpayer to prove the existence of controlled experiments, accurate measurements, and the rigorous testing of formulated hypotheses against empirical evidence.

In Revelations Research Ltd., the appellant conflated working in an emerging scientific field—artificial intelligence—with conducting a scientific experiment. The appellant's president presented the project's ambitious goals, including a cellular network model of natural intelligence and a ten-year plan of milestones, supported by expert opinion that neural networks were an emerging technology whose outcome could not be assured in 1985; however, the Court found it unnecessary to review particular aspects of Mr. Madryga's evidence because it had no hesitation in accepting Dr. Davies' contrary evaluation. As Dr. Peter C. Davies testified, the only plan he found in the appellant's documentation was a ten-year plan overview, which listed goals without any mention of how they would be achieved and which, in his view, might have served as part of a business plan but was not a research plan. Dr. Davies received no information setting out initial hypotheses or any proposed means of determining their truth or falsity, detailed notes of research work were not produced, and the Court found that it had not been established that there was any systematic investigation of the kind described in Sass Manufacturing Ltd., which contemplates repeatable experiments in which the steps, the changes made and the results are carefully noted. According to Dr. Davies, the work was not carried out in any systematic, scientific manner, as Mr. Madryga had ideas he believed might prove fruitful but no plan for implementing them, so that the taxpayer's activities amounted to unstructured conceptual exploration rather than scientific research or experimental development.
Absence of Verifiable Technological Uncertainty and Hypothesis-Driven Testing

A closely related technical deficiency in Revelations Research Ltd. is sometimes framed as a failure to prove technological uncertainty, but the Court made no finding on that criterion: the appellant's experts opined that considerable technological uncertainty existed at the outset, and the Court decided the appeal instead on the weight of the evidence and the absence of a proven systematic investigation. Under the Canadian SR&ED framework, technological uncertainty exists only where the probability of achieving a given technical objective or performance benchmark cannot be known or determined in advance on the basis of standard practice, publicly available scientific knowledge, or routine engineering experience. Furthermore, the resolution of that technological uncertainty must be pursued with the objective of achieving a technological advancement—that is, generating new scientific or technological knowledge that advances the underlying baseline of technology.

During the Tax Court proceedings, the divergence between Professor Snelgrove's favourable opinion and Dr. Davies' disqualifying assessment exposed a critical legal pitfall that frequently ensnares software and AI claimants. Professor Snelgrove, whose area was signal processing, opined that there would certainly have been considerable technological uncertainty at the outset that the targeted real-time performance could be obtained, and Dr. Rennick likewise considered that the outcome of the neural-network work could not be assured in 1985; the Court, however, found this evidence somewhat restrained and only partially supportive of the appellant. Canadian tax law does not grant Investment Tax Credits merely because a taxpayer's business operates near a frontier of academic interest. As confirmed in Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen (citing Revelations Research Ltd. and Canalerta Technologies Inc.), whether an activity constitutes SR&ED is to be considered not in its constituent parts but as a whole, as part of a systematic investigation or search. Revelations Research Ltd. did not establish that its work advanced knowledge: Dr. Rennick could not comment on whether the neural engine it constructed was technically correct or a scientific advancement, and Dr. Davies testified that nothing significant had been accomplished and that the research team was inadequate in size and in the credentials of its members for the project's central neural-network work.
Deficiencies in Contemporaneous Documentation and Evidentiary Corroboration

In Canadian tax litigation, the initial onus of demolishing the Minister's assumptions of fact rests squarely on the appellant taxpayer. In Revelations Research Ltd., the taxpayer's documentary case was weak: detailed notes of research work were not produced, Dr. Rennick's report recorded that Mr. Madryga had shredded all working papers for commercial security and that the small team did not write reports, and the Court attached no evidentiary weight to pages of computer printouts in the three volumes assembled for the appeal. When Dr. Peter C. Davies examined the appellant's documentation to determine whether any portion of the project qualified, he found no part of it eligible, pointing to the absence of a research plan, the absence of stated hypotheses and means of testing them, the lack of any systematic, scientific conduct of the work, and the inadequacy of the research team.

The appellant attempted to bridge this evidentiary chasm at trial through the oral testimony of its company president and the retrospective expert evaluations of Professor Snelgrove and Dr. Rennick, both dated October 21, 1991. The Tax Court of Canada was not persuaded: it held that the appeal fell to be decided by the weight or credibility of the evidence, that the evidence of Professor Snelgrove and Dr. Rennick did not of itself satisfy it that the project was SR&ED, and that, to the extent Mr. Madryga's evidence was in meaningful conflict with that of Dr. Davies, the latter prevailed, an outcome consistent with a principle later echoed in Canalerta Technologies Inc. v. M.N.R. [1992] and Hadad v. M.N.R. [1994]: oral assertions by an interested corporate officer, uncorroborated by contemporaneous experimental records, lab notebooks, source code progression logs, mathematical models, or test failure analysis created at the time the work was allegedly performed, are insufficient to discharge the taxpayer's legal burden of proof. Moreover, an expert witness cannot manufacture primary facts that do not exist in the contemporaneous record. Because the underlying factual substratum of contemporaneous experimental logs, architectural specifications, and empirical test results was missing, the opinions of Professor Snelgrove (who expressly limited his clear judgment to the data-acquisition component within his signal-processing expertise) and Dr. Rennick (who relied on Mr. Madryga's information at face value and was not qualified as an expert on neural networks, the project's central activity) lacked an objective evidentiary anchor, prompting the Court to prefer the evidence of Dr. Davies.
Failure of Expenditure Nexus, Supporting Activity Substantiation, and Contractual Clarity

Beyond the core scientific eligibility of a project under paragraphs 2900(1)(a) through (c) of the Income Tax Regulations, a claimant seeking deductions under section 37 and ITCs under section 127 (refundable in certain cases under section 127.1) of the Income Tax Act must establish a strict legal and financial nexus between the claimed expenditures and the eligible experimental activities. Under the later version of the definition (paragraph 2900(1)(d), which post-dates the 1986 year at issue, whose counterpart then required only that such activities be undertaken directly in support) in the Regulations, ancillary activities such as computer programming, mathematical analysis, engineering design, and data collection are eligible only if they are "commensurate with the needs and directly in support" of the core basic research, applied research, or experimental development.

In Revelations Research Ltd., the appellant relied exclusively on paragraph 2900(1)(c), and because it failed to establish that its project fell within that paragraph, there was no eligible core activity that any supporting work could be directly in support of; the Court did not need to, and did not, examine individual categories of expenditure. Furthermore, the decision makes no findings about time-tracking, project-level accounting, or contracts; the dispute concerned entitlement to a Part VIII refund against Part VIII tax of $15,750,000 assessed on a $31,500,000 designated amount, and it was resolved entirely on whether the project itself constituted scientific research and experimental development. Where a taxpayer claims refundable tax credits without maintaining segregated project cost accounting, explicit statements of work defining technical uncertainties, and verifiable links between employee or contractor remuneration and specific experimental tasks, the entire claim is vulnerable to total disallowance.

body.text: Section 4: Applied Remedial Case Studies in Canadian SR&ED Practice

To translate the judicial principles of Revelations Research Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue into actionable compliance protocols for Canadian corporate taxpayers and technical advisors, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic R&D projects vulnerable to the exact legal and evidentiary pitfalls identified by the Tax Court of Canada. Each case study demonstrates step-by-step how to restructure project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and experimentation tracking to withstand CRA audit scrutiny and satisfy the statutory requirements of subsection 248(1), section 37, and section 127 of the Income Tax Act (Canada).
Case Study 1: Neural Architecture and Domain-Specific Artificial Intelligence Inference Engine
Baseline Vulnerability Scenario

An Ontario-based Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC), "AetherLogic AI Inc.," is developing a proprietary multi-modal neural inference engine designed to execute real-time predictive diagnostics on edge-computing microprocessors with severe memory and thermal constraints. In its initial posture, AetherLogic AI Inc. commits the exact errors of Revelations Research Ltd. The company's Chief Technology Officer drafts a post-hoc T661 SR&ED claim narrative asserting that because edge-based generative AI is "state-of-the-art," all software engineering hours spent building the platform qualify as SR&ED. The engineering team uses standard agile sprint tickets focused on product features ("Build user dashboard," "Optimize model latency") without recording baseline technological limitations, formal hypotheses, or failed experimental iterations. Furthermore, AetherLogic AI Inc. engages two external machine-learning consultants under generic time-and-materials software development agreements and receives a commercial pilot payment from an industrial client without segregating funded commercial deliverables from internal experimental research. Under the Sass standard applied by the Tax Court, and the kind of evaluation by Dr. Peter C. Davies that the Court accepted, in Revelations Research Ltd., a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) would disallow 100% of the claim due to the absence of proven technological uncertainty, lack of systematic experimentation, and unsubstantiated expenditure linkages.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Baseline Benchmarking

To cure these fatal deficiencies and satisfy the Tax Court of Canada's evidentiary standard, AetherLogic AI Inc. must begin by overhauling its project governance prior to commencing experimental coding. The corporation must establish an internal SR&ED Governance Committee led by its Principal AI Architect that mandates a formal "State-of-the-Art Baseline Dossier" before Project Day 1. This dossier documents exhaustive literature searches, public benchmark evaluations—such as testing standard quantization methods including INT4 AWQ and GPTQ on the target ARM Cortex-A microprocessor—and empirical proof that existing public algorithms result in a 42% degradation in diagnostic recall when compressed below 120 megabytes of RAM. By documenting that standard computer science methodologies cannot reconcile memory footprint with diagnostic precision, the taxpayer transforms a vague commercial goal into a legally cognizable technological uncertainty under Canadian law. Governance protocols must simultaneously bifurcate the project into an "Eligible Core Experimental Track" investigating novel mixed-precision tensor decomposition algorithms under paragraphs 2900(1)(b) and (c) (now subsection 248(1)) and an "Excluded Commercial Track" covering UI/UX design, API wrappers, and database ingestion.
Step 2: Implementing Contemporaneous Technical Documentation Architecture

In the second phase of remediation, to avoid the evidentiary gaps highlighted by Dr. Davies (no research plan, no stated hypotheses, no detailed research notes) in Revelations Research Ltd., AetherLogic AI Inc. must replace retrospective narrative summaries with an automated, immutable contemporaneous documentation pipeline integrated directly into its Git version control and MLflow tracking servers. Every experimental cycle must be logged in a standardized "Hypothesis-Experiment-Analysis-Conclusion" (HEAC) technical template dated at the exact time of execution. Each record must state the mathematical hypothesis—for example, that applying non-uniform Hessian-weighted eigenvalue pruning to attention layers 4 through 9 will preserve F1-scores above 0.94 while reducing peak RAM allocation by 38%—specify the exact dataset and control parameters, capture automated telemetry outputs such as memory profiling graphs, loss convergence curves, and quantization error matrices, and document a rigorous scientific analysis of why the experiment succeeded or failed.
Step 3: Re-engineering Contractual Terms and Funded Research Insulation

In the third phase, to secure the deductibility of expenditures under section 37 and ITC eligibility under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, legal counsel must overhaul all third-party agreements. Subcontractor agreements with the external machine-learning consultants must be redrafted as "Canadian SR&ED Subcontract Statements of Work" explicitly stating that the work is performed in Canada on behalf of AetherLogic AI Inc., detailing the exact mathematical analysis and experimental programming tasks under paragraph (d) of the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) (formerly paragraph 2900(1)(d) of the Regulations as amended after the period at issue in Revelations Research), and vesting 100% of all intellectual property—including failed experimental data and source code—exclusively in AetherLogic AI Inc. Simultaneously, the commercial pilot agreement with the industrial client must be restructured into a standard commercial licensing contract for the finished software product, explicitly stipulating that the client is purchasing a non-exclusive licence to a commercial deliverable, bears no financial risk for R&D failure, and acquires no rights to the underlying experimental AI architecture, thereby insulating AetherLogic AI Inc. from reductions of qualified expenditures for contract payments (as defined in subsection 127(9)) under subsection 127(18) of the Act.
Step 4: Deploying Granular Experimentation and Cost-Nexus Tracking

As the fourth remedial measure, AetherLogic AI Inc. must implement a bi-weekly time-tracking ledger that maps every employee and contractor hour directly to specific Git commit hashes and MLflow experiment IDs. Supporting activities—such as writing custom C++ CUDA kernels or generating synthetic test datasets—are tagged with a mandatory cross-reference to the specific core experimental hypothesis they directly support, satisfying the "commensurate with the needs and directly in support" requirement of the current definition (discussed in Data Kinetics Ltd.; Revelations Research Ltd. applied the earlier "directly in support" wording and did not reach this issue).

body.text: Case Study 2: Autonomous Mechatronic Control System and Embedded Sensor Fusion
Baseline Vulnerability Scenario

A British Columbia-based industrial engineering corporation, "Pacific Kinematics Ltd.," designs automated timber-processing robotics and attempts to claim SR&ED tax credits for developing an adaptive electro-hydraulic actuator and multi-sensor fusion control system capable of operating in sub-zero, high-vibration sawmill environments. Like the appellant in Revelations Research Ltd.—where the Court heard three experts all learned in computer science, specializing respectively in signal processing (Prof. Snelgrove), data acquisition and real-time systems (Dr. Rennick), and artificial intelligence and neural networks (Dr. Davies)—Pacific Kinematics Ltd. operates at the intersection of mechanical hardware and algorithmic control. However, the company conducts its development on the live commercial production floor using shop-floor trial-and-error adjustments. Engineers swap hydraulic valves and tweak proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller gains until the machine operates acceptably, keeping only commercial shop work orders and final CAD drawings. Furthermore, the company claims the entire cost of the commercial timber-processing machine as an SR&ED expenditure and relies on a university engineering professor's two-page letter stating that the machine is "highly innovative". Under Sass Manufacturing Ltd. and Revelations Research Ltd., the Tax Court of Canada would reject the claim on the grounds that shop-floor trial-and-error tuning lacks systematic experimental methodology, the professor's letter lacks an empirical foundation, and routine commercial engineering cannot be claimed as SR&ED.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Isolating System-Level Uncertainty

To transform this vulnerable mechanical and control-systems project into a legally defensible Canadian SR&ED claim, Pacific Kinematics Ltd. must first establish a formal Engineering Research Review Board that separates commercial machine fabrication from experimental development before physical prototyping begins. The board must document why standard industrial engineering practice and off-the-shelf electro-hydraulic control equations fail under simultaneous sub-zero fluid viscosity shifts (from 20°C down to −40°C) and 150 Hz structural frame resonance. By modelling the coupled fluid-structure interaction mathematically first, the engineering team defines a precise technological uncertainty: the inability of classical linear PID and Kalman filter architectures to prevent harmonic actuator oscillation when hydraulic bulk modulus varies non-linearly with rapid thermal transients. This governance gate ensures that the project seeks a genuine technological advancement in non-linear mechatronic control theory rather than routine mechanical troubleshooting.
Step 2: Instituting Contemporaneous Technical Documentation of Empirical Testing

Addressing the core critique in Sass Manufacturing Ltd. and Revelations Research Ltd. that scientific research requires controlled experiments and accurate measurements, Pacific Kinematics Ltd. must next institute a mandatory "Experimental Test Rig Protocol." Rather than making unrecorded adjustments on the shop floor, engineers must document each iterative test series in a serialized Digital Engineering Notebook. Each entry must record the analytical mathematical model predicting system damping, the exact physical configuration of the environmental test chamber, high-frequency oscilloscope and accelerometer data streams sampled at 10 kHz, and a comparative variance analysis explaining why empirical phase-margin measurements diverged from the mathematical simulation. If an external academic consultant is retained to review the work, the expert must be provided with the raw oscilloscope datasets, mathematical derivations, and failure logs so that any expert report is grounded in primary empirical facts rather than abstract praise.
Step 3: Reforming Contractual and Capital/Materials Expenditure Structuring

In the third phase, to comply with Canadian statutory rules governing materials and overhead under section 37 and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, legal and tax advisors must strictly segregate custom experimental prototypes from commercial production assets. Contracts with third-party machine shops fabricating custom hydraulic manifolds must explicitly designate the components as "Destructive Experimental Test Articles—Non-Commercial" and specify the metallurgical and geometric tolerances required to test the fluid-resonance hypothesis. Furthermore, the company must track and classify materials rigorously between "materials consumed"—rendered virtually valueless during destructive cold-chamber fatigue testing—and "materials transformed" into a prototype that may later be sold or converted to commercial use, thereby managing exposure to SR&ED recapture rules under subsections 127(27) to (35) of the Income Tax Act.
Step 4: Enforcing Structured Experimentation Tracking and Shop-Floor Segregation

In the final phase, Pacific Kinematics Ltd. must implement an ERP work-order coding system that physically and financially isolates experimental testing from commercial assembly. Shop-floor technicians and mechanical engineers must log time against dedicated "SR&ED Experimental Test Codes" only when fabricating destructive test coupons, instrumenting the environmental test rig, executing controlled test matrices, or performing mathematical signal-processing analysis. Routine CAD drafting of standard structural frames, commercial PLC wiring, and post-experiment reliability testing are logged to excluded commercial cost centres, ensuring an unimpeachable audit trail that satisfies the strict evidentiary standards of the Tax Court of Canada.

Ad-hoc shop-floor trial-and-error tuning of valves and PID gains without defining a scientific problem.

Mathematical System-Constraint Specification proving failure of linear Kalman/PID models under thermal transients.
Technical Documentation
Reliance on final CAD drawings and a generic two-page endorsement letter from a university professor.
Serialized Digital Engineering Notebooks recording mathematical predictions vs. 10 kHz empirical sensor telemetry.
Dated Test Rig Logs, accelerometer/oscilloscope data files, and mathematical variance analyses.

Claiming the entire cost of a commercial timber-processing machine without accounting for commercial use or recapture.
Procurement contracts designating custom parts as destructive test articles; strict tracking of consumed vs. commercial materials.
Vendor POs for experimental test rigs; Material Consumption & Scrap Certificates for destructive testing.
Experimentation Tracking
Blending commercial machine assembly hours with troubleshooting time on generic shop work orders.
Segregated ERP cost-accounting codes separating controlled test-chamber runs from commercial fabrication.
Timecard logs mapped to specific environmental chamber test runs and paragraph 248(1)(d) supporting analysis.

body.text: Section 5: Strategic Synthesis for Canadian Tax Counsel and Technical Advisors

The Tax Court of Canada's ruling in Revelations Research Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue remains one of the most instructive cautionary tales in Canadian R&D tax jurisprudence. As one of the earliest Canadian judicial decisions to evaluate artificial intelligence research in the context of SR&ED tax incentives (specifically, entitlement to a Part VIII refund), the ruling stripped away the mystique of emerging computer science terminology and subjected AI development to the same rigorous scientific standard applied to traditional physical engineering in Sass Manufacturing Ltd.

For contemporary Canadian tax practitioners, corporate counsel, and technical advisors, three enduring legal imperatives emerge from Revelations Research Ltd. and its judicial progeny (Canalerta Technologies Inc., Hadad, Promac Informatique Inc., and Data Kinetics Ltd.). First, technological novelty in the marketplace or participation in an advanced field such as artificial intelligence does not create a presumption of SR&ED eligibility; the taxpayer must prove that it conducted a systematic investigation by means of controlled experiment or formal analysis to resolve a specific technological uncertainty. Second, the evidentiary burden before the Tax Court of Canada cannot be discharged through retrospective executive testimony or high-level academic endorsements when the underlying record is devoid of contemporaneous experimental documentation. Third, as demonstrated by the Court's reliance on Dr. Peter C. Davies' forensic technical critique over the restrained and only partially supportive evidence of Professor Martin Snelgrove and Dr. Donald F. Rennick, the Tax Court of Canada evaluates SR&ED claims through a strictly empirical lens—demanding dated hypotheses, measurable test protocols, verifiable analytical logs, and cogent evidence of a systematic investigation (the accounting nexus between claimed expenditures and eligible work being a requirement of later law and practice rather than a point decided in Revelations Research).
